title: Period pain
intro: Period pain, or dysmenorrhoea, is cramping pain in the lower abdomen before or during menstruation. It is very common, especially in teenagers and young women. Most period pain is not a sign of disease and can be eased with heat, exercise and painkillers, but severe pain deserves investigation.

sections.heading: Why it happens
paragraphs: Before and during a period, the womb produces substances called prostaglandins that make its muscle contract to shed the lining. High levels cause stronger contractions and pain, and can also cause nausea, diarrhoea or headaches. This primary period pain often starts in the first years after the first period and tends to lessen with age and after childbirth.

sections.heading: When another cause is possible
paragraphs: Secondary period pain arises from conditions such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids or pelvic infection. It often starts later in life, gets worse over time, lasts longer than the bleeding, or comes with heavy bleeding, pain during sex or between periods. These need medical assessment.

sections.heading: What you can do
paragraphs: Warmth from a hot-water bottle or warm bath relaxes the muscle. Gentle exercise, such as walking, yoga or swimming, may help. Relaxation and adequate sleep can ease symptoms. Some women find TENS devices helpful.

sections.heading: Medicines
paragraphs: Anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen work well when taken at the first sign of pain or a day before, if periods are predictable, and taken with food. Paracetamol is an alternative. Hormonal contraception, including the pill, hormonal coil or implant, reduces prostaglandin production and often lightens periods and pain. Discuss options with your doctor.

sections.heading: When to see a doctor
paragraphs: Seek advice if pain disrupts school, work or daily life, does not respond to simple measures, begins suddenly in adulthood, or comes with fever, unusual discharge or very heavy bleeding. Examination and ultrasound can look for underlying causes. Pain is not something you have to accept as normal.

examples.title: Planning ahead
examples.text: Imagine your period pain is worst on the first day. You could take ibuprofen with food as soon as cramps start, use a warm pad and plan lighter activities if possible.

examples.title: Raising it with a doctor
examples.text: Suppose your pain has gradually grown worse over several years. You might keep a diary of pain, bleeding and effects on daily life and ask about endometriosis.
